## Six-hundred-and-sixty-seventh round: the pk2 reader and the texture decodes in Rust -- the Jangan entry from 9.9 s to 6.1 s warm, the centre cell from 3.4 s to 1.7 s

The user asked (2026-09-30) whether loading is faster with pk2 decrypting, loading and parsing done
in Rust through a GDExtension. Their players are on slower PCs than theirs, and they will emulate
low-end CPU and storage once this is shown to work. This round is that spike. It has four parts:
measure where the parse time goes, port the top of it, prove parity on the real archives, and A/B
one build both ways, warm and cold. Build, test and toolchain: native/README.md. The A/B recipe:
client/tools/README.md, "Native readers A/B". Next ports: docs/TODO.md, "Native (Rust) readers".

Labels: MEASURED (on the render box, real archives at /opt/sro-files/client, Jangan spawn
97/168 at 1002,1020, 1280x720, loading screen forced), READ (the Godot 4.2.2 source), INFERRED,
OURS.

### 1. Where the time went: ranked, before porting anything

`client/scripts/pk2/parse_profile.gd` (new, `OPENSRO_PARSE_PROFILE=1`) times every pk2 directory
read, with the disk read and the Blowfish decrypt apart. It also times every file read, every path
lookup (`ObjectLoader.find_file`) and 23 parser entry points, by thread, and prints `PARSEPROF`
lines. Two runs gave the same picture within 3 %; these are run 2's entry window, from the drain's
start to its LoadTimings summary (MEASURED):

| key | main thread ms (calls) | workers ms (calls) |
|---|---|---|
| **pk2 directory decrypt** (`pk2.dir_decrypt`, GDScript Blowfish) | **2,637 (1,051 blocks)** | **896 (315)** |
| `ddj.to_image` (texture decode) | **1,242 (606)** | 202 (329) |
| `bms.parse` | 330 (330) | **977 (652)** |
| `pk2.find_file`, beyond its directory reads: the name scan and waiting on the reader's lock | 162 | **569** |
| `mapm.parse` | 17 | 531 (24) |
| `nvm.parse` | 13 | 478 (24) |
| NPC text tables (`npc_models` 218, `ui_table` 185, `npc_codes` 109, `npc_positions` 27) | 539 | 0 |
| `bms.to_arrays` | 59 | 70 |
| `pk2.dir_entries` (slicing a decrypted block into entries) | 56 | 19 |
| `ban.parse` / `bsr.parse` / `bsk.parse` | 55 / 34 / 24 | 16 / 27 / 2 |
| `pk2.read_file` (153 MB) | 46 | 127 |
| `pk2.dir_io` (3.5 MB of directory blocks off the disk) | 3 | 2 |
| `tile2d.parse` | **1.8** | 0 |

Before the entry, the boot tables add another 192 ms of directory decrypt on the main thread and
143 ms on the workers.

What the table says:
- **The pk2 directory decryption WAS the cost.** The brief said it was not, because only directory
  blocks are encrypted. That is true, but there are 1,366 of them in one entry. Each 2,560-byte
  block is 320 Blowfish block decrypts in GDScript, about 2.5 ms a directory block (MEASURED). That
  is 3.5 s of CPU, 2.6 s of it on the main thread, before counting the worker tasks queued behind
  `Pk2Reader._lock` while it is held through a decrypt (the 569 ms row).
- **The centre cell's `tiletable 707` was never the tile table.** `tile2d.parse` takes 1.8 ms. The
  rest is the lookup of `navmesh\tile2d.ifo`, which decrypts the whole `navmesh` folder, the
  largest in Data.pk2. Native, the lap is 7 ms (§4).
- `ddj.to_image`'s cost is its two per-pixel GDScript loops (uncompressed textures through their
  channel masks, and the half-float `q`). The DXT branches already hand off to Godot's C++.
- Disk reads are a rounding error warm: 3 ms for every directory block and 46 ms for 153 MB of
  files.

So the port was the pk2 reader (directory decrypt, name index, lookup, read) and, as the top
parser, `ddj.to_image`'s per-pixel decodes. `bms.parse`, mapm, nvm and the text tables are
next, in that order (docs/TODO.md).

### 2. What was built

- **`native/`**: a Rust crate. `godot` is pinned to `=0.5.5` with `api-4-2` and
  `experimental-threads`, Rust is 1.98.1, and Cargo.lock is committed.
  - `src/core/` is plain Rust with no Godot type: Blowfish, the pk2 archive and the ddj decodes.
    This keeps it binding-agnostic, as the user asked, so the same code can sit behind a C ABI
    and be linked statically if antivirus objects to the DLL.
  - `src/gd.rs` is the thin gdext layer: `SrNativePk2` and `SrNativeParsers`. It returns packed
    arrays or one Dictionary per call, never a Variant per element.
  - The archive decrypts each directory once and indexes it by lower-cased name. As
    `find_file`'s scan does, the first entry of a name wins. Reads are positional
    (`pread`/`seek_read`), so threads share no cursor and need no lock to read.
- **The client** never names a native class as a type. `client/scripts/pk2/native_assets.gd`
  finds them through `ClassDB.class_exists`/`instantiate`, so every script compiles and runs
  without the library.
  - `Pk2Reader` keeps its API. With the library it hands directories, lookups and reads to the
    native handle; without it, nothing changes.
  - `DdjReader.to_image` sends its two per-pixel branches to native when available. A native
    refusal falls through to the GDScript branch, which reports its own error.
  - `OPENSRO_NATIVE=0` forces GDScript in a build that has the library. The client logs which
    path it took: `NativeAssets: native readers ON|OFF (...)`.
- **`client/opensro_native.gdextension`** gives the linux.x86_64 and windows.x86_64 paths
  (`res://native_bin/`, git-ignored). Libraries are build output: `native/build.sh [windows]`.
  `.gitignore` covers `native/target/`, `client/native_bin/`, `*.so`, `*.dll`, `*.dylib` and
  `*.rlib`.
- **Without the library** (MEASURED: a copy with the `.gdextension` but no `native_bin`, which is
  CI's case and a player's without the DLL), Godot 4.2.2 prints four `ERROR` lines and carries on:
  `Can't open dynamic library`, `GDExtension dynamic library not found: .../libsrrevamp_native.so`,
  `Failed loading resource: res://srrevamp_native.gdextension` and `Error loading extension`.
  `check_scripts.gd` then prints `ALL LOAD` and exits 0, all 179 suites pass, and the client logs
  `NativeAssets: native readers OFF (library not loaded)`.
- **The export presets exclude the `.gdextension`** (READ, `editor_export_platform_pc.cpp`, 4.2.2).
  The exporter adds the library a `.gdextension` names to the shared objects and fails the export
  when its `da->copy` fails. The release workflow builds no library yet, so without the exclusion
  every tagged release would have failed. The workflow itself is unchanged.
- **`perf_gate.sh` gained `--ab-env "VAR=value"`**, which runs the base side on the head's own
  copy with those variables, so one build is compared both ways. It also gained `--cold` (§5).
  `remote_godot.sh` and the gate ship `client/native_bin` when it is built.
  `NO_NATIVE=1 remote_godot.sh ...` ships no library and removes the box's copy.

### 3. Parity on the real archives (MEASURED)

`client/tools/native_parity.gd` reads the four archives both ways in one process (202 s):

| archive | directories / entries compared | lookups compared (case/slash/missing variants) | files read, bytes compared | per-pixel `.ddj` decodes compared |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Data.pk2 | 2,734 / 75,872 (every one) | 70,261 (16,974) | 25,846 / 1,868,030,264 | 1,052 (rgb32 804, rgb16 232, rgb8 12, rgb24 4) |
| Map.pk2 | 101 / 19,511 | 9,428 (2,664) | 3,491 / 302,173,729 | 38 (rgb32) |
| Media.pk2 | 168 / 23,002 | 11,453 (3,207) | 21,812 / 726,889,128 | 9,653 (rgb32 5,935, rgb16 3,696, rgb24 14, rgb8 8) |
| Particles.pk2 | 40 / 5,871 | 3,356 (906) | 1,934 / 105,798,627 | 134 (rgb32 128, rgb16 2, q 4) |
| **total** | **3,043 / 124,256** | **94,498** | **53,083 / 3.00 GB** | **10,877** |

- Every directory of every archive is compared entry by entry: name, kind, offset and size.
- Lookups cover every file in a folder of up to 300 entries and every 25th in larger ones. Every
  10th also gets an upper-cased, a `/`-separated and a missing variant.
- Every 7th file is compared byte for byte, plus every `.ddj`.
- Every uncompressed or `q` texture is decoded both ways and compared as RGBA bytes.

Result: `PARITY PASS`, with **0 mismatches**.

**The negative.** `cargo build --features parity-negative` makes a library with two deliberate,
subtle bugs: it never reads a directory block's 20th slot, and it leaves BGR unswizzled. Shipped to
a separate box copy, it fails both checks (MEASURED):

```
FAIL Data's 27 entries over two chained blocks agree entry for entry (27 / 26)
FAIL 32-bit BGRA decodes to the same RGBA both ways ([48, 32, 16, 64, ...] / [16, 32, 48, 64, ...])
FAIL 16-bit ARGB1555 decodes to the same RGBA both ways (...)
FAIL 24-bit, no masks recorded decodes to the same RGBA both ways ([3, 2, 1, 255] / [1, 2, 3, 255])
4 FAILURES
FAIL Particles.pk2: dir '' has 21 entries in GDScript, 20 native
FAIL Particles.pk2: dir '' entry 18: GDScript (map.rar, dir false, @150203305, 462877) native (co, dir true, @140892261, 0)
FAIL Particles.pk2: dir 'co' has 55 entries in GDScript, 53 native
PARITY FAIL 5354
FAIL Map.pk2: dir '' has 190 entries in GDScript, 181 native
PARITY FAIL 18373
```

`cargo test --features parity-negative` fails 4 of its 9 tests too.

Tests:
- `cargo test --no-default-features`: 9 pass. They cover Schneier's Blowfish vectors (the same 9
  as blowfish_test.gd), the pk2 variant, a synthetic plain and encrypted archive with a chained
  folder and a case-variant duplicate, and every ddj branch and fallback.
- `client/scripts/pk2/native_assets_test.gd` (new) runs on synthetic input both ways:
  - an encrypted chained archive: directories, 8 lookup variants, bytes, and 1,600 concurrent
    native lookups and reads from 8 WorkerThreadPool tasks;
  - four textures;
  - without the library, the fallback.
- Box suites, with the library: `remote_godot.sh check` ALL LOAD (445 scripts) and `tests` 179
  suites, 0 failing. The existing pk2, asset-source and object-loader suites then run through the
  native path. Without it (`NO_NATIVE=1`): ALL LOAD, 179 suites, 0 failing.

### 5. The gain, cold (MEASURED)

The box's container cannot drop the page cache: `/proc/sys/vm/drop_caches` is read-only there
(`Read-only file system`). `--cold` instead evicts each `*.pk2` with
`posix_fadvise(POSIX_FADV_DONTNEED)` before every run and records `fincore` afterwards. Godot, the
project and the shader cache stay cached, so this is cold archives, not a cold machine.

`--ab-env OPENSRO_NATIVE=0 --sites jangan,mobs --cold`, 3 runs a side. `fincore` read
**0 pages** of the five archives resident after every one of the 12 evictions.

```
perf gate: base working tree with OPENSRO_NATIVE=0 vs head working tree (1280x720, median of 3 run(s), cold page cache)
jangan  frame ms   base 9.49  head 9.72  (+0.2)  SAME
jangan  entry ms   base 10118  head 6230  (-3888.0)  FASTER
jangan  freeze ms  base 3477  head 1752  (-1725.0)  FASTER
jangan  hitches    base 5  head 5  (+0.0)  SAME
mobs    frame ms   base 10.93  head 10.71  (-0.2)  SAME
mobs    entry ms   base 11371  head 7135  (-4236.0)  FASTER
mobs    freeze ms  base 3482  head 1896  (-1586.0)  FASTER
mobs    hitches    base 5  head 5  (+0.0)  SAME
```

Jangan, median of 3, cold against warm:

| | GDScript cold (warm) | native cold (warm) |
|---|---|---|
| entry | 10,118 (9,966) | 6,230 (6,097) |
| centre cell | 3,424 (3,339) | 1,748 (1,656) |
| `tiletable` | 711 (710) | 10 (7) |
| `textures` | 103 (93) | 13 (5) |
| `models` | 683 (659) | 246 (217) |

**Cold costs this box about 0.1-0.2 s an entry, either way.** `lsblk` in the container lists a
Samsung 970 EVO Plus NVMe, and an entry reads about 157 MB: 153 MB of files and 3.5 MB of
directory blocks (PARSEPROF bytes). On this box the load is CPU-bound, warm or cold. On a slow
disk, the 157 MB is what an entry pulls off it. The native reader reads the same bytes and does not
change that (INFERRED from the identical byte counts). The user's storage emulation is what will
measure it.

### 6. Windows (MEASURED here; NOT run on Windows)

`native/build.sh windows` cross-compiles for `x86_64-pc-windows-gnu` with mingw-w64 13 (Ubuntu's
`gcc-mingw-w64-x86-64`). The output is `srrevamp_native.dll`, 2.3 MB stripped, a PE32+ DLL. Its
export table is exactly `gdext_rust_init`, the `.gdextension`'s entry symbol. It imports only
system DLLs: `KERNEL32`, `msvcrt`, `ntdll`, `USERENV`, `WS2_32`, `bcryptprimitives` and
`api-ms-win-core-synch-l1-2-0`. No MinGW runtime DLL has to ship beside it.

Why GNU and not MSVC (`cargo-xwin`):
- It builds from distribution packages on the Linux runner, without fetching Microsoft's CRT and SDK.
- The GDExtension interface is a C ABI, so the compiler that built Godot does not matter.

What the user should check on the PC: `Initialize godot-rust (API v4.2..., runtime v4.2.2...)`
and `NativeAssets: native readers ON (library loaded, opensro_native 0.1.0)` in the log. The DLL is
unsigned. SmartScreen or antivirus may quarantine a new unsigned DLL, and the client then simply
runs in GDScript. The fixes are signing, or the static link the core was kept Godot-free for. How
CI would build it on `kakariko-runner` is in native/README.md, "Exports and CI". This round does
not change it.

### 7. OPEN

- **Not run on Windows.** The DLL is built and its exports checked, nothing more.
- **Not shipped.** The release workflow builds no library, and the presets exclude the extension.
- **The parsers not ported**, ranked in docs/TODO.md: `bms.parse` first, then mapm and nvm, then
  the NPC text tables. The boot tables (about 1.1 s) are not profiled function by function.
- **Cold is cold archives only**, for the reason in §5. The user's low-end storage emulation is the
  real test.
- **perf_gate's frame number reads into loading** when an entry leaves fewer than 30
  once-a-second samples after it (base Jangan run 1, §4). That is a gate issue, not a cost of this
  round. It is noted here, not fixed.

### 8. Review follow-up (round 667's review: M1-M3, L1, L5, L6)

The review had no HIGH findings, and the reviewer reproduced the gain in its own lane (entry 9,800
-> 5,958 ms, freeze 3,408 -> 1,673). It asked for the fixes below. Round 668 (CI and shipping the
DLL) takes L2, the MPL notice and the CI build.

**M1. The ordinary gate could credit any round with the native speed-up.** `perf_gate.sh` shipped
`client/native_bin` to the head copy whenever the working tree had one, and a base revision never
has one. The rule now (perf_gate.sh header; client/tools/README.md, "Native readers A/B"):
- In base/head mode, NEITHER side gets the library or the `.gdextension`.
- In `--ab-env` mode, one copy has the working tree's library. `--head REV` and a tree without
  `client/native_bin/libopensro_native.so` are refused.
- Every run's `NativeAssets: native readers ...` line is read back. In `--ab-env` mode a head run
  must say ON; any other run must not.

MEASURED, d7b4aba's gate against this one, `--sites jangan --runs 1 --frames 1500`:

```
d7b4aba, base/head mode, client/native_bin built -- the native gain credited to the round:
jangan  entry ms   base 10023  head 5983  (-4040.0)  FASTER      (head log: native readers ON)
now, the same:
  jangan head run 1: frame 9.81 ms, entry 9945 ms, freeze 3388 ms, 5 hitch(es), native readers OFF
jangan  entry ms   base 9932.00  head 9945  (+13.0)  SAME

d7b4aba, --ab-env with no library built -- GDScript against GDScript, passed as a comparison:
jangan  entry ms   base 9812  head 9861  (+49.0)  SAME           exit 0
now: --ab-env: no client/native_bin/libopensro_native.so -- run native/build.sh first, or both sides read in GDScript   (exit 2)
now, --ab-env --head HEAD: --ab-env needs the working tree's built library: --head REV carries none, so both sides would read in GDScript   (exit 2)
now, PERF_SELFTEST_DROP_LIB=1 (the copy shipped without its library):
  jangan head run 1: FAIL native readers OFF, this side must be ON -- the comparison would not be what it says   (exit 1)
```

**M2. A stale library was used silently.** `client/native_bin` is git-ignored and survives a pull,
and the box's copy survived every `remote_godot.sh` sync. The fixes:
- **An interface number.** `API` in `native/src/core/mod.rs` and `NATIVE_API` in
  `native_assets.gd` are the same constant, now 2. The client uses a library only when its `api()`
  returns exactly that. Otherwise it reads in GDScript and logs one line.
- **Sync mirrors the box copy.** `sync_client` deletes the box's `native_bin` first and ships it
  again only if the local tree has one.

MEASURED:
- **This client with d7b4aba's own library**, sha256 `1a082918...`, which has no `api()`:
  `NativeAssets: native readers OFF (library REFUSED: API 0, this client needs API 2 -- a stale
  library, rebuild it with native/build.sh)`. native_assets_test.gd: `ok  a refused library is not
  used`.
- **The new suite on d7b4aba's client:** `SCRIPT ERROR: Parse Error: Static function
  "api_verdict()" not found in base "NativeAssets".` and `Cannot find member "NATIVE_API"`.
- **The sync, with no library in the local tree:** d7b4aba's `remote_godot.sh sync` left
  `box native_bin: libopensro_native.so`. Now: `ls: cannot access '.../native_bin': No such file
  or directory`.

**M3. An entry's size went straight to an allocation.** `Archive::read` allocated `size` bytes as
the archive stated them, up to 4 GiB, and Rust aborts on a failed allocation. Now:
- the file's length is recorded at open;
- every read is clamped to it, so the result is what `FileAccess.get_buffer` gives;
- a read past the end returns nothing;
- the remaining allocation is fallible (`try_reserve_exact`).

New test `oversize_entry_reads_only_what_the_file_holds`. On d7b4aba:

```
panicked at src/core/pk2.rs:380:9: allocated 4294967295 bytes for a 10521-byte file
under `ulimit -v 3000000`: memory allocation of 4294967295 bytes failed ... (signal: 6, SIGABRT: process abort signal)
```

Now it passes, under the limit too.

**L1. A mask wider than 56 bits overflowed `value * 255`.** The arithmetic is now u128. New test
`wide_masks_do_not_overflow`; on d7b4aba: `panicked at src/core/ddj.rs:26:10: attempt to multiply
with overflow`.

**L5.** native_assets.gd named `--base-env`; the flag is `--ab-env`. **L6.** The Linux library
needs **GLIBC_2.34** (`dlsym`, `pthread_key_*`), because it was built on Ubuntu 24.04. This is
noted in native/README.md; where the release's library is built is round 668's decision.

**Re-run after the fixes (MEASURED):**
- `cargo test`: 11 pass. With `parity-negative`: 5 of 11 fail.
- Box `check`: ALL LOAD. `tests`: 179 suites, 0 failing.
- `native_parity.gd`: PARITY PASS, the same counts as §3.
- `perf_gate.sh --ab-env OPENSRO_NATIVE=0 --sites jangan`: entry 9,941 -> 6,258 ms and freeze

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-sixth round: the deploy guide matches the release -- the skills re-import, the nest files' permissions and the full monster population -- and the server stops keeping a brain for every monster a player has passed

The final release review of the monster epic (rounds 653-665) found the deploy guide out of step
with the release and a few small server faults. Server and docs only, so no performance gate.
Round 665 (the retail resurrect choices) ran in parallel. This round does touch files it also
edits -- `session/monsterai.go`, `session/status.go` and `deploy/README.md` -- in other functions
and sections; round 665's review found the merge clean. (Corrected in the review follow-up: the
first commit said nothing here touched its files.)

Labels: READ (the binaries, the decompiles), MEASURED (here, on the dev machine), INFERRED, OURS.

### 1. The deploy guide (deploy/README.md, server/README.md)

- **M1, the monster population.** The guide still called `-nest-swapped-stand-in` "the setting for
  a public server" and quoted round 660's 7-10 fps. It now says what the user decided (round 660's
  review, "DB numbers now"): opensro-01 runs the full population with the stand-in OFF, round 664
  having made the dense fields hold 60 fps; the stand-in is an optional OURS fallback.
- **M2, the skills re-import.** The guide said the skills CSV "grows to 90 columns". It has 91:
  column 90 is StatusParams (`refdata/csv.go`, the column list and `f[90]`), stored as
  `skills.status_params`. A table imported before round 659 loads '' in every row and no skill
  lands a status, silently. The guide now says the release needs the skills re-exported and
  re-imported, with the two checks (`status_params <> ''` above 0; `ai_attack_chance > 0` about
  26650). The server also warns at every boot while no skill carries status params (§2).
- **M3, the nest files' permissions.** The image runs as distroless `nonroot` (`server/Dockerfile`);
  the export runs under `umask 077` and scp keeps 0600, so the container cannot read the CSVs and
  the boot crash-loops. The guide now has `chmod 755 ~/opensro-data/nestdb; chmod 644
  ~/opensro-data/nestdb/*.csv`, and the boot error says so (§2).
- **Stale lines corrected**: "No unique is placed in the world yet" (they are, with `-full-map` and
  `-nest-db-dir`, round 661); "Who spawns where does not change" (only without `-full-map`); "a
  client that stops reading stalls the tick" (not since round 662's per-session queue); the Monster
  AI section's pre-660 description (the DB tactics, battle, aggro, uniques, the area of interest);
  "4,068 rows" (this release's boot logs `matched=4063`; the review's number, not re-derived here);
  step 2's `rm` left `itemdata.txt`, `skilldata.txt` and `leveldata.txt` behind (added).
  server/README.md had the same staleness in `-monsters-csv`, `-monster-ai`, `-monster-sleep` ("5x5
  regions") and `-nest-swapped-stand-in`; corrected.
- **The opensro-01 procedure**: a numbered section, "Deploying the monster-epic release to
  opensro-01 (round 666)", with the seven steps the final reviewer verified (build with
  `CGO_ENABLED=0`; export; copy skills/monsters/npcpos and the importer; copy exactly the five shard
  files and chmod; re-import the skills and run the checks; the override's command with
  `-monsters-csv -nest-db-dir -full-map` and the six monster flags, no stand-in and no
  `-unique-respawn`; the expected boot lines: `nest DB loaded ... tactics=1743 nests=16381
  hives=1170 ai_skill_tactics=132 skills=36144`, `placed=10104`, seven `unique rotation`, seven
  `unique hatched`). The expected numbers are the reviewer's, not re-measured in this round. The
  `docker compose exec postgres psql` line of step 5 is ours (the compose file's service, user and
  database), not one the reviewer ran.

### 2. Server fixes (OURS unless labelled)

- **M4, sleeping brains are dropped** (`session/monsterai.go`). Brains were walked every pass (the
  insistent scan and the reconcile loop) and freed only at a death, so a player crossing the map
  left a brain per monster passed. Now a brain whose monster falls asleep (no watcher, nothing
  insistent) is dropped, and what it must keep is filed as a `brainMemory`: the state it slept in
  (IDLE or WANDER; BATTLE, HOMING and a status-held monster never sleep), its entry time and dwell,
  the target and the run home, the heading, the cooldown (`lastSwing`, `swungReuseMs`), tactics
  timers 1 and 6, the aggression roll (a re-roll could turn a passive monster aggressive), and a
  unique's damage total and triggers (an HP trigger fires once a life). The wake rebuilds the rest
  from the monster -- home, tactics, radii and detection are arithmetic over `combat.Monster` --
  and resumes the machine in the filed state with the new `ai.Machine.Resume` (no OnEnter, no new
  dwell, no rng draw). The leg stays in the monster hub, as before. The status hold still wakes a
  filed monster (`addHeld` asks `hasBrain`, which counts a filed memory), and so does a blow: a
  damage-over-time tick whose caster walked away is the monster's struck event (round 659), and the
  retained brain took it and chased; `wakeStruck` rebuilds a filed brain before the blow is drained,
  so it still does (`TestFiledMonsterTakesADoTBlow`, a guard, not a negative). Memories of monsters that
  die asleep are swept 64 a pass (`asleepSweepPerTick`); ids are never reused, so a stale one can
  never wake into another monster.
  MEASURED (a throwaway test, not committed: 66,000 monsters given brains by one sleep-off pass,
  then sleep on with one player): **base 66,000 brains, 6.05 ms a pass; this round 4 brains,
  0.063 ms**. (The review's 13.2 ms was its own run and machine.)
- **Strike workers end with the fight.** A monster's strike goroutine lived as long as the monster
  (the review counted 14 left in r1 from `handStrike`). `leaveBattle` now queues the brain, and
  after the pass's swings are handed over the channel of each brain that is still out of BATTLE is
  closed (`retireWorkers`); the worker ends after what it holds, and the next fight's first swing
  starts a new one. A sleep closes it too, as a death did.
- **A DoT kill arms the party nest.** `dealMonsterTick` never called `noteMonsterKilled`; it now
  does, with the tick's credited applier as the killer (0 for a tick that names nobody, which
  counts no party -- `statuseffect.SourceRule`, READ), as a killing blow does.
- **M2's boot warning.** `statusParamsWarning` (cmd/server): with no skill carrying status params,
  every boot logs `skills store has NO status params (N skills, 0 with status_params): no skill
  lands a status ... RE-EXPORT skills.csv ... (91 columns, column 90 StatusParams) and RE-IMPORT
  it ...`, naming the monsters too under `-monster-ai`. Status effects have no switch
  (`RunStatusEffects` is started unconditionally), so the check runs on every boot, from both the
  PostgreSQL store (`CountSkillsWithStatusParams`, `WHERE status_params <> ''`) and the in-memory
  one.
- **M3's boot error.** `nest.openDBFile` wraps a refused open: `... permission denied: chmod 644
  the nest DB's CSVs and chmod 755 their directory (the server runs as a nonroot user ...)`,
  still wrapping the `fs.ErrPermission`. MEASURED here, both builds run as `nobody` against a
  root-owned 0600 `Tab_RefTactics.csv`: base `err="open .../Tab_RefTactics.csv: permission
  denied"`; this round `err=".../Tab_RefTactics.csv: permission denied: chmod 644 the nest DB's
  CSVs and chmod 755 their directory ..."`.
- **`-monster-sleep`'s help** said "the 5x5 regions"; it is now built from `session.AOIRadius` and
  `combat.CellSpan` ("the 3x3 blocks of 320 units", round 664's READ window) so it cannot drift again.
- **The densest-window boot line** took whichever tied cell the map's iteration met first; a tie
  now goes to the lowest cell (zone, X, Z) (`densestWindow`).

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-fifth round: a player killed among monsters is no longer trapped reviving and dying -- retail's two resurrect choices, "the specified point" taking it back to town

The final release review (run r3) watched a GM under `-player-dead-state` auto-revived in place
at 366.0, 397.0, 428.0 and 459.0 s and killed again within 0.1-0.5 s each time, losing 933,800
EXP per death; `/tp` is refused while dead, and a level-30 player looped the same way. OpenSRO
only revived in place: round 549's 30 s auto-revive, and a Revive button that sent an empty
`OpRevive`. This round read retail's resurrect flow in both binaries and built its choices.

Labels: READ (SR_GameServer.exe / sro_client.exe: the decompiles, `srv.asm`, `sro_client.asm`,
and wide strings read out of the client executable on the render box), MEASURED, INFERRED, OURS.
The reading is filed in `docs/protocol/character_state.md`, "The resurrect choices (round 665)",
and `server/internal/session/deadstate.go`, "THE CHOICES".

### 1. What retail does (READ)

- **The window**: message box kind 3 (`UI_SILKMALL::FUN_00644c90` case 3). The line
  `UIIT_MSG_MSGBOX_ASK_SELF_REBIRTH_2`, "Choose a method to resurrect yourself.", and two buttons.
  Control 0xc9 is `UIIT_MSG_MSGBOX_REBIRTH_POINT_BUTTON`, "Resurrect at the specified point."
  (`push 0xd9d340` at `0x6455ed`). Control 0xca is `UIIT_MSG_MSGBOX_REBIRTH_STANDING_BUTTON`,
  "Resurrect at the present point.", while the player's max level (`FUN_009d4d70`, the byte at
  `player+0x20d8`) is at most 10 (`cmp al,0xa; ja` at `0x645688`), and
  `UIIT_MSG_MSGBOX_REBIRTH_HELP_BUTTON`, "Waiting for other player's help." (`0xd9d2f8`) above.
- **The request**: the box's event map (`0xeb5e88` 0xc9 -> `FUN_0063b6e0`, result 1; `0xeb5eb0`
  0xca -> `FUN_0063b8b0`, result 0) -> `FUN_00777dd0` -> `FUN_00797d90(kind 3, result)`. At max
  level 10 or under, result 1 sends **0x3053 {u8 1}** (`push 0x3053` at `0x797e30`) and the other
  button **{u8 2}** (`0x797eec`); above 10, result 1 sends {u8 1} and the other button sends
  **nothing** (`jne 0x798a61` at `0x797efd`). The opcode is 0x3053: the "0x7053" in earlier rounds
  was the project's `0x7000 | op` precedent, never a read.
- **The handler** (`GObjPC_HandleResurrectMsg_053`, `0x50fee0`, round 550's reading re-checked):
  state 2 only; option 2 revives in place only while `GetMaxLevel` is under 11 and otherwise does
  nothing; option 1 is `GObjPC::Revive(0)`. No reply message of its own.
- **The return point**: `Revive(0)` -> `CGObjPC::FUN_004e08a0` looks `_CHAR.AppointedTeleport` up
  as a ref object (`FUN_004260b0`), its `+0x190` teleport record read by `FUN_004e0a40` ->
  `FUN_00407760` (region +0x20, X/Y/Z +0x26/+0x28/+0x2a, world +0x48: a gate's arrival), and
  leaves through slot `0x378` (`CGObjPC::vslot_222`, `0x4df590`: the destination stored, the PC
  taken out of the world by `FUN_004df050` to enter again there). `Revive(0)` sets no state and no
  pool; the re-entry's load path restores a stored zero pool to 40 % (`GObjPC::FUN_004e1120`).
  The point is set by a gate's "Designate as return/recall point" line (interaction id 7); that
  service's server side and a new character's default are NOT read.
- **Leaving dead**: `FUN_004df050` (`cmp al,0x2` at `0x4df129`) resolves the return point
  (`call 0x4e08a0` at `0x4df188`) and saves it (`0x4df194`..`0x4df1ae`).
- **No timed revive in the open world**: of `GObjPC::Revive`'s thirteen call sites (listed in the
  doc; this entry first said ten -- the review found `0x52d9ff`, `0x5f0e6f` and `0x662b17`) none is
  on the PC's one-second tick (`CGObjPC::PeriodicUpdate`, `0x52aa90`); only a fortress war
  (`PeriodicUpdateInSiege`) and the battle arena (`CBattleArenaInfo::vslot_004`, `0x662a20`, a
  `GetTickCount` deadline then `Revive(1)`) revive on a timer. The scripted warp job
  `AJStateChanger::vslot_002` (kind 0xb / 0) also calls `Revive(0)`; its creators were not traced.
- **The handler's other arms** (the review): an empty 0x3053 takes the PC out of the world
  (`FUN_004df050(4)`) before any option is read, and a cause-2 death (`+0x72d`, no penalty)
  revives in place whatever the option and level. OpenSRO's dead state is only a monster's kill
  (cause 3); its empty request is the pre-665 client's (OURS, the level's one choice).
- **Protection**: `Revive(1)` sets body mode 2 (invincible) for 6.0 s (`0xb45b78`; 11.0 s,
  `0xb45bb8`, in the other world kind); a return to the return point is a world re-entry, where
  `CGObjPC::vslot_391` (`0x4df9e0`) sets body mode 2 for the world's own time (slot `0x70`, not
  read). Not modelled (OPEN).
- **EXP**: the penalty is charged once, at the kill (`GObjPC_OnDeath`); neither revive path
  charges anything.

### 2. What shipped

Server (`session/deadstate.go`):

- `OpRevive` carries retail's option byte (`ReviveOption`). **Option 1** moves the dead character
  to its return point first (`returnToPoint` -> `warpTo`: the mover's `OpChangeZoneResult`, the
  zones' left/entered, the position saved) -- still dead, so no monster can take it between the
  two -- then revives it there at the load path's pools (`reviveWith`: HP `trunc(0.4 x MaxHP)`, at
  least 1; MP kept, or 40 % if empty). **Option 2** revives in place (round 550's 1 +
  `trunc(0.4 x MaxHP)`) at level 10 or under (`PresentPointMaxLevel`) and is refused above it.
- **The return point is OURS**: OpenSRO keeps no `AppointedTeleport`, so it is the place every
  character enters the world at, `spawnZone`'s arrival (`returnPoint`).
- **The 30 s in-place auto-revive is removed** (`RunAutoRevive`, `autoReviveTick`,
  `AutoReviveAfter`; cmd/server no longer starts it).
- An empty request (a client before this round) is option 2 at level 10 or under and option 1
  above it (OURS), so an old client neither loops nor is refused.
- A character leaving dead is saved at its return point (`savedPlace`, READ above), on disconnect
  and on server stop, under `-persist-position`.
- **Flag off** (`-player-dead-state` off, the default): the kill's instant respawn is moved to the
  return point after the kill's own messages (`returnAfterKill`, called by the strike worker, the
  attacker's counter and the status tick) -- OURS, the dead state compressed with option 1; before,
  the player came back at 40 % where it fell.

Client: the dead window has retail's line and two buttons, their text resolved from the player's
own textuisystem.txt (`HudPanels.show_revive_prompt(line, level)`; the second button is the
present point at level 10 or under, else the disabled help button), and `NetClient.revive(option)`
sends the byte. `OPENSRO_QA_REVIVE_OPTION` picks the QA hook's button (default 1).

OURS in the window: the talk prompts' box instead of the retail message-box art; our death line
kept above retail's; the help button disabled and the box left up, where retail's click closes it
(INFERRED: its result goes through `FUN_00777dd0`), because no one can resurrect another player
in OpenSRO yet.

- **H1, option 1 with a failing store crashed the server.** `ReviveHandler`'s option-1 arm
  declared `moved, err :=`, shadowing the switch's `err`; a failed revive then reached
  `sendRevived` with a nil character, and the gateway does not recover a handler's panic, so every
  player was disconnected. Now `werr`, and `sendRevived` answers "revive failed" for a nil
  character. The round's other new code has no shadowed error (`reviveWith` redeclares in its own
  scope; `returnAfterKill`, `savedPlace` and the guard return none).
  Test: `TestReviveOptionOneWithAFailingStoreIsRefused`.
- **M1, a stale move could pull her back (flag off).** `returnAfterKill` warps from a strike
  worker or the status tick, while her client, never told she died, may still be walking; a step
  handled after the warp put her back where she fell. Now the move home arms a **return guard** on
  her session (`warpHome`: armed before `warpTo`, bound to the hub's `Arrival` stamp after it):
  until a move arrives within 400 units (x and z; OURS) of the arrival or the zone's client spawn
  spot (`worldmap.LandingSpotFor`), moves elsewhere are dropped; a later zone change or two minutes
  (OURS, `warpLandingGrace`) ends it. The guard lives on the session, so it goes with the
  connection. The periodic position save no longer writes the place back

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-fourth round: dense monster fields hold 60 fps -- a player is sent only the monsters of the 3 x 3 blocks around it, as retail sends them, and a 2,500-monster crowd draws at 40 fps instead of 6

Round 660's follow-up measured the full map with the shard DB: 1,378 bodies drawn at the Europe
starter field (region 108/77) ran the client at 100 ms a frame, and 2,412 at the densest window
(cell -116/8) at 143. The user chose to ship that population ("DB numbers now"), so the client
has to hold it. The round read what retail sends and draws, measured where the frame went, and
fixed both ends.

Labels: READ (SR_GameServer.exe / sro_client.exe, the decompiles and objdump on the render box),
MEASURED (render box, 1280x720), INFERRED, OURS.

### 1. What retail shows (READ; docs/protocol/monster_ai.md, "What a player is sent: retail's message blocks")

**The server's visibility window is the 3 x 3 message blocks of 320 units around the player's
block** -- a 960-unit square reaching 320 to 640 units from the player on each axis. Ours was 5 x
5 regions of 1,920 (round 656, OURS): 100 times the area.

- A field region (`CRgnTerrain`) holds 6 x 6 `CMsgBlockTerrain` (0x24 blocks of 0x98 bytes at
  +0x2c, the constructor 0x53a850).
- A position's block is its region-local (x, z) divided by **320.0** (the double at 0xb45ae8;
  `CRgnTerrain::vslot_006` 0x53ad30, `fdiv` at 0x53ad90, each index asserted 0..5).
- Each block is linked once to its 8 neighbours (the (dx, dz) table at **0xc64090**, read back
  with objdump), across region lines (`CRgnTerrain::vslot_016` 0x53ab90 -> `FUN_0053ac20` ->
  the neighbour region by 0x430900, the block `(i + 6) % 6`), into the list at block+0x10
  (`CMsgBlock` slot 5, 0x5336e0).
- An object put into a block (`CMsgBlock` slot 2, 0x534340) is, for each neighbour and the block
  itself, sent that block's objects if it is a player (the group spawn 0x3017/0x3018, 0x533e70)
  and announced to its players (0x3015, 0x533f70); taken out (slot 3, 0x5344b0), it is despawned
  to the same nine (0x3016, 0x534050).

**The client draws what it holds.** The per-frame entity list (`CEntityManagerClient::vslot_011`
0x9c4770) lists every object; the object draw (0x9c4aa0) tests the frustum and, with graphics
option 0x17 on, passes distance / **800.0** (0xd83080, `fdiv` at 0x9c4c05) to the model draw as a
**mesh** LOD factor (`pFDB->Indices[iLOD]`). No distance rule on animating a character was
found. Round 655's 2,020 pose range stays OURS; the animation LOD below is OURS.

### 2. Where the frame went (MEASURED, before any fix)

A new QA hook, `OPENSRO_QA_MOBSPLIT=<frames>`, prints one line of the frame's split every
`<frames>` rendered frames (`MonsterCrowd.Split`): physics steps a frame, the clip tick
(`_tick_idle_animations`) and inside it the pose and the sound calls, the height stepping, the
build pump, the minimap, the renderer's own CPU and GPU time, draws and primitives, and
Godot's `TIME_PROCESS` (which holds the draw). `OPENSRO_QA_MOBSPLIT_OFF=pose,sound,labels,
collide,mesh` switches parts of every body off for the A/B. The stress case is the new gate
site `crowd`: the Jangan spawn with **2,500 monsters of 17 real species within 1,920 of the
player** (`OPENSRO_QA_MOBS=2500 OPENSRO_QA_MOBS_SPREAD=1920`). int/mob 46559e0's code, medians
of the steady lines:

| run | ms/frame (`--print-fps`, median) | physics steps a frame | clip tick a step | renderer CPU / GPU | what it shows |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| all | 167 | 8.0 (capped) | 16.3 ms | 6.6 / 6.4 ms | |
| no clip sounds advanced | 45 | 2.7 | 7.3 ms | 6.9 / 6.7 | **advancing 2,500 bodies' sounds: 9.1 ms a step** |
| no posing | 143 | 8.0 | 13.5 ms | 1.7 / 1.6 | **posing the 70 in view: 2.8 ms a step, plus the re-skinning in the draw** |
| no posing, no sounds | 18.5 | 1.0 | 4.4 ms | 1.4 / 1.4 | **the loop's own tests over 2,500 bodies: 4.4 ms** |
| no monsters | 9.6 | 1.0 | 0.3 ms | 0.8 / 0.9 | the Jangan scene itself |

The meshes / plates / colliders A/B in that regime (200 ms each, slower than "all") overlapped
another lane's render and is noise; taken again at the fix's midpoint (the tick already once a
frame, 39.2 ms): meshes hidden 30.9 ms, name plates and HP bars hidden 37.8 (within noise --
they are already range-culled at 80), click colliders removed no change. So the bodies' meshes
cost ~8 ms there, and nearly all of it is the posed ones (posing off: renderer CPU 6.6 -> 1.7).

**The multiplier:** the clip tick ran in every PHYSICS step. At 60 steps a second a 100 ms frame
runs six steps and a 176 ms frame the capped eight, so every millisecond of per-step cost was
paid up to eight times -- the slower the frame, the more steps, the slower the frame. Round 660's
100 and 143 ms were this spiral. The minimap walked every body in every step too (2.2 ms a step
at 2,500). Height stepping, the build pump and the label and collider nodes were not the cost.

### 3. The fixes

**Server (READ):** `combat.CellSpan` = 320 (retail's block; the cell index was region-sized) and
`session.AOIRadius` = 1: a player is listed, spawned, moved, struck and despawned only the
monsters of the 3 x 3 blocks around its own (`server/internal/combat/cells.go`,
`server/internal/session/aoi.go`). The enter/leave pushes, the paged list and the sleep are
round 656's, on the new cell. The awake area around each player shrinks with it (the sleep stays
OURS). Round 656's tests are rescaled to the block (their positions were region multiples);
`nest660_test`'s densest window is now one nest's 6 (the two synthetic nests stand 1,216 apart).

**Client** (`client/scripts/world/monster_crowd.gd`, new; `World3D.gd`; `anim_sounds.gd`):

1. **The clip tick once per rendered frame** (`MonsterCrowd.TickGate`): it runs in the first
   physics step of a frame with every step's time since the last run -- no second of any clip is
   lost, and at 60 frames a second nothing changes. OURS, as retail has no physics step
   (INFERRED from its once-a-frame entity list, 0x9c4770).
2. **Clip sounds only within hearing** (`MonsterCrowd.hearable`): a body's sound tracks are
   advanced only within 600 of the listener (READ: the core plays no positioned sound beyond 600,
   0xda98fc, `SoundTable.culled`). A body going out of hearing is rested once
   (`AnimSounds.rest`) and comes back without firing what passed while it was away.
3. **Posing without the bone search** (`MonsterCrowd.pose_at`): a monster body's clips map
   tracks to bone indices once per clip and model (every body is a duplicate of its species'
   template, `META_LAYOUT`), and the skeleton recomputes its transforms once at the end of the
   frame instead of at every pose. The pose is bone-for-bone the old one (the test compares them).
4. **The loop's tests from a cache** (`MonsterCrowd.CullCache`): a culled skeleton's radius, hide
   flag, resting flag and slot are read once; the range and frustum tests are MonsterDraw's,
   written out; a loop neither in view nor in hearing does nothing more; one that was quiet at
   its last test is tested every second frame (`recheck_due`; OURS: a body coming into view is
   posed at most one frame late).
5. **Far bodies posed less often** (`MonsterCrowd.pose_interval`, OURS): every frame within 300 of
   the camera, every second frame to 900, every fourth to the 2,020 range, each on its own slot.
   A skipped frame is not a slower clip: the next pose is where the clip has got to.
6. **The minimap once a rendered frame**, fed only the bodies that can land in its sign circle
   (the circle's radius at the drawn zoom, x1.01; the circle's own test still decides).

**What changed in `monster_draw.gd`: nothing.** Round 661's Templates change is untouched; the
round's client rules live in the new `monster_crowd.gd`, and World3D sets one meta on a monster's
skeleton at build (`MonsterCrowd.META_LAYOUT` = its model path) next to round 655's metas.

| physics steps a frame | 8.0 | 1.5 |
| clip tick a frame | 130 ms | 7.3 ms (pose 2.0 for 46 bodies, sounds 1.2 for the ~190 within 600, the loop 4) |
| minimap a frame | ~18 ms (2.2 a step x 8) | 1.7 ms |

- Retail's mesh LOD (distance / 800, option 0x17) is not drawn: the LOD index sets were not read.
- The animation LOD and the quiet recheck are OURS; retail's character update rule is unread.
- The READ window is the field's; the object regions' blocks (`CMsgBlockObject`) and any object
  sent from farther were not read. The sleep stays OURS.

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-third round: the game no longer stops hearing the server when a big monster list arrives behind a burst -- the client reads what has arrived instead of waiting for a whole message

Round 662's live check (WORLD_ISSUES round 662 §4) found a client fault the server had been
hiding. `packet_reader.gd` read a frame's payload only once `get_available_bytes()` covered all of
it. A server that wrote its queue in one write wedged the real client for good after a
`/goto jangan` in a dense crowd. Round 662 fixed the server side, by writing a frame per write.
This round fixes the reader, so no server write pattern can do it again. Client network code
runs every frame, so the performance gate was run.

### 1. The fault (MEASURED in round 662; READ for TLS)

- **TCP.** `ss -tmi` on the frozen client showed a full receive buffer:
  `skmem:(r137152,rb138172,...)` held only 31,250 bytes of data. The kernel charges a segment's
  whole memory until it is read to its end, and loopback carried the big writes as ~52 KB segments
  (`rcvmss:52224`). The reader waited for 32,735 bytes (a list page) to be "available". That never
  happened, because the reader would not read, so the window stayed shut and neither side moved.
- **TLS (READ, Godot 4.2.2 source).** `StreamPeerTLS.get_available_bytes()` is
  `mbedtls_ssl_get_bytes_avail` (`modules/mbedtls/stream_peer_mbedtls.cpp`): only the bytes left in
  the current decrypted record, at most 16,384. So over TLS a payload larger than one record was
  never all "available", and the old reader could not read any frame over 16 KB (the tests in §3
  show it: `0 of 2 frames decoded`). Nobody met it because nothing uses TLS: the login screen
  connects without it (`Login.gd:300`, `use_tls` left false), and `deploy/` sets no TLS (READ).

### 2. What was built (OURS unless marked)

- **`PacketReader` reads into its own buffer** (`client/scripts/net/packet_reader.gd`). Each
  `poll()` polls the peer, then, while its buffer does not hold a whole frame, reads what the peer
  has, up to `READ_CHUNK` = 64 KB. It then cuts out the next whole frame.
  - A TCP peer is asked for `min(get_available_bytes(), 64 KB)`.
  - A TLS peer's count is only the current record's, so once that is read the reader polls the
    peer again, which decrypts the next record if it has come, and reads that (review follow-up;
    the first version asked a TLS peer for a blind 64 KB read, which allocated 64 KB on every idle
    poll).
  - A peer that is no longer connected is not asked (a closed peer answers every count or read
    with an engine ERROR line). A read that ends in `ERR_FILE_EOF` (a clean close) returns
    nothing, without an error line.
- **The frames are decoded exactly as before.** Size is the field's low 15 bits, then the opcode.
  Header bytes 4 and 5 (RollingByte/ChecksumByte) are ignored, as `Packet.encode()`'s note
  says: the server sends neither. Frames come out in arrival order, one per `poll()`.
  `NetClient._process` still drains `poll()` until it returns null (`net_client.gd`: comments only).
- **The bound.** The reader reads only while it lacks a whole frame, and drops the consumed bytes
  before each read, so its buffer holds less than one frame plus one read:
  `MAX_BUFFER` = 6 + 32,767 + 65,536 = 98,309 bytes. The largest the test measured was 98,299.
  (The first version compacted only once 64 KB had been consumed, so its buffer could reach about
  164 KB, and its comment undercounted: the review's finding. It measured 131,072 under the
  mutant below.) The copy on each compaction is only the one unfinished frame, done once per
  frame taken.

### 3. Tests (`client/scripts/net/packet_reader_fragments_test.gd`)

- **Fragment patterns.** A fake peer (a `StreamPeerBuffer` handed its bytes a fragment per
  `poll()`) carries 11 frames: small ones, an empty one, a 32,735-byte page, a 32,767-byte frame,
  and the small ones after them. The patterns are:
  - one byte at a time;
  - 3-byte fragments, which split every header;
  - 7-byte fragments;
  - all frames in one chunk;
  - 52 KB pieces, as loopback carried round 662's writes;
  - 16,384-byte pieces, as one TLS record at a time.

  Each must decode to exactly the frames sent, in order, byte for byte.
- **Round 662's wedge.** The same frames in 52 KB pieces go through a receive buffer that holds
  at most 31,250 unread bytes (ss's figure). The page, and every frame after it, must decode.
- **The bound.** Six full-size frames wait at once. The reader's `_buf` itself must stay under
  98,309 bytes (read with `get("_buf")`).
- **It reads only while it lacks a frame.** 20 small frames and 200 KB more wait at once. After the
  first `poll()`, the next 19 must be served from the buffer without reading from the peer.
- **The Size flag bit.** A frame whose Size field is `0x8000 | 5` carries 5 bytes, and the frame
  after it is found.
- **TLS in one poll.** With every record of the page already in the client's socket, the page
  must come out of the first `poll()`. NetClient drains until the first null, once a game frame,
  so this is one game frame. A reader that reads only the current record takes 2.
- **TLS close.** After the server's `close_notify`, the reader, polled as NetClient polls it, returns
  nothing. The runner checks that no ERROR line appears between the test's two marker lines.
- **Real TLS loopback.** A self-signed certificate is made in the test. A 32,735-byte page and the
  frame after it must decode within 3 s. The client trusts the test's certificate
  (`client_unsafe(cert)`), because with no chain Godot falls back to its default CA bundle, which a
  `--script` run has not loaded ("SSL module failed to initialize!", `init_client`).
- **NEGATIVE against int/mob 1ea6b02's `packet_reader.gd`** (copied over the lane's copy on the
  box, run, then restored; MEASURED):

```
ok  one byte at a time: every frame decodes identically
...
ok  16,384-byte pieces (one TLS record at a time): every frame decodes identically
FAIL a 32,735-byte page through a receive buffer holding 31,250 bytes decodes, and every frame after it -- 7 of 11 frames decoded
ok  the reader holds at most one frame plus one 64 KB read (held 0 bytes)
FAIL TLS: a 32,735-byte page and the frame after it decode within 3 s -- 0 of 2 frames decoded
2 FAILURES
```

  The fragment patterns pass on the base as well: with no buffer limit, waiting works. They pin
  that the new reader decodes identically.
- **On the branch:** all 9 checks `ALL PASS`. `remote_godot.sh check` on the tree merged onto int/mob
  46559e0: ALL LOAD (439 scripts). `remote_godot.sh tests`: 177 suites, 0 failing; round-trip suites such as `packet_reader_test.gd`
  (split frames, two frames in one read) pass unchanged.

### 4. The live A/B (MEASURED, render box, `/var/tmp/reader663/live.sh`)

Round 662's forced-order scenario:
- **The server is a debug build, not committed.** The writer is put back to one write per take (the
  behaviour that froze the old client), plus a 60 ms sleep at the top of the list handler, so the
  area of interest's view move nearly always beats the list request.
- **The run:** `-qa-spread-monsters 6000 -qa-spread-radius 5` with the six monster switches on.
  One real client enters at the Jangan spawn, runs `/goto donwhang`, `/goto jangan`, then three
  `/spawnunique`.
- **"Came through"** means that after the return to Jangan the client printed the list report and
  all three `GM REPLY: spawned unique ...` lines, which the server logged as sent in every run.
- **"Enters first"** means the ~1,250 monsters arrived as spawn pushes before the list.

**On round 662's branch (server built from feat/sendq662 with the debug change):**

| run | client | enters first | after the return |
|---|---|---|---|
| a1 | int/mob's reader | yes (1,251 pushes) | **wedged**: no list report, no GM reply for `/heal` or the three `/spawnunique` |
| b1 | this round's reader | yes (1,254) | came through: `server reports 1250 monster(s)`, every GM reply, the three uniques listed |

**On the merged tree (server built from int/mob 46559e0 with the debug change).** The client is the
round-663 client merged onto 46559e0. For the "old" runs the lane's copy of `packet_reader.gd` was
replaced with 46559e0's and restored afterwards, so the two clients differ only in the reader.

| run | reader | enters first | after the return |
|---|---|---|---|
| a2 | old | yes (1,258 pushes) | came through (`server reports 1254`, 3 GM spawn replies) |
| a3 | old | yes (1,255) | **wedged**: 2 list reports in all (entry and Donwhang), 0 GM spawn replies |
| a4 | old | no (4 pushes; the list won the race) | came through |
| b2 | new | yes (1,252) | came through (`server reports 1248`, every GM reply) |
| b3 | new | yes (1,260) | came through (6 list reports, 3 GM spawn replies) |

The old reader's wedge is a matter of chance, not a certainty. It needs the enters first, and then
a receive buffer whose part-read segments hold less than the page. Of the three old-reader runs
that took the enters first, a1 and a3 wedged and a2 came through. All three new-reader runs that
took the enters first came through. On the server side, every run's writer debt peaked under 1 ms,
there was no stall line, and the only disconnect is the script ending each client. The fragment
suite's receive-buffer case (§3) is the deterministic version.

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-second round: a player whose connection is slow can no longer freeze everyone else's monsters -- the server writes to each player from that player's own queue

The monster-world epic (2026-09-30). Round 656's reviews (§7-§9) left one thing standing: a
`Send` wrote on the caller's goroutine, so a client that kept reading, but slower than it was
written to, held every goroutine that wrote to it -- the AI tick (which fans out to every watcher
in turn), the single respawn scheduler, every other player whose blow sends it a damage or a
death -- for up to its 10 s blocking budget before it was closed. The budget could not go lower,
because a healthy client stops reading for 3.3 s or more while a load freezes its main thread.
Server-only round (gateway and send layer); no client code, so no performance gate.

### 1. What was built (OURS)

- **A per-session outbound queue and writer** (`gateway.go`). `Send` encodes the frame into the
  session's queue -- its rolling byte and checksum drawn there, in call order, and its bytes
  copied, so the caller may reuse the packet -- and returns without touching the socket. The
  session's own writer goroutine (`writeLoop`, started when the gateway accepts the connection)
  takes everything queued and writes it out **a frame per write** (`writeFrames`; §4 says why not
  in one write). A payload too large for one frame is still
  refused synchronously, as `proto.Write` refused it (round 656's list negative depends on that).
- **Order.** Frames reach the wire in the order `Send` was called for that session. The monster
  wire lock keeps its meaning unchanged: a check and its send are one step under it, and queue
  order is wire order. **`SendBatch`** queues several frames as one, so no frame from any other
  goroutine comes between them: the paged monster list with its motion pages
  (`monsterlist.go:176`) and a monster's enter with its leg (`aoi.go:499`).
- **The bounds.** A Send that would take the queue past **`gateway.SendQueueLimit` = 2 MB**
  closes the session (reason `queue`); so does the writer's blocked time passing round 656's
  budget (`SendBlockBudget` 10 s draining 10 s per 60 s, unchanged, reason `budget`) or one write
  passing `SendTimeout` (10 s, reason `timeout`). Every later Send returns `ErrSendStalled` at
  once. The bounds are read into the session when it connects, so a test that changes them races
  no live writer.
- **The end of a session drains** (`closeAfterDrain`). When the read loop ends (the client hung
  up, a handler returned an error, the server is stopping), OnDisconnect runs, then what is still
  queued is written for up to **`SendDrainTimeout` = 2 s** (OURS), then the connection is closed and
  the writer is waited for. So a frame sent just before a handler's error still reaches the
  client, as it did when Send wrote synchronously. `Session.Close` still closes at once.
- **Memory.** The writer exits when the session closes; the queue is set to nil, and a buffer
  bigger than 64 KB is not kept for reuse after it is written.
- **The accounting.** Besides round 656's debt, longest write and bytes, each session records the
  most bytes ever waiting in its queue and the most bytes Sent in any 4 s (`SendBurstWindow`, 16
  buckets of 250 ms). New peaks past 64 KB are logged ("send queue peak", "send burst peak",
  again at each doubling), and the disconnect line carries `send_queue_peak` and
  `send_burst_peak`.
- **Round 657's per-session notice queue (L4) is folded in.** `broadcastUniqueNotice` now calls
  `Send` for each character; the notice-only `noticeQueue` and its drainer goroutines are gone.
  Its tests pass unchanged.
- A `NewTestSession` still panics on Send (no connection), as before: one test drives a panic
  through a push that way (`TestPanickingPushLeavesTheWireLockFree`).

### 2. Every Send caller, classified (READ from the code at 1ea6b02; line numbers are the branch's)

Round 656's builder wrote that every caller relies on "the frame is on the wire when Send
returns". Checked, that claim is wrong: no caller reads the socket, and none depends on the frame
having been written. What callers do rely on is four narrower things, each of which the queue
keeps: **order** per session (kept: queue order is call order), **contiguity** of a multi-frame
sequence against other monster messages (kept by the wire lock, and now against everything by
`SendBatch`), a **synchronous error** for an oversized payload (kept), and **delivery before a
close** (kept by the drain). 354 call sites outside the gateway (an AST walk of every `.Send(` and
`.SendBatch(` in non-test code):

- **Multi-frame sequence, needs contiguity -> `SendBatch`** (2): `monsterlist.go:176` (the list's
  pages and the motion pages, under the wire lock), `aoi.go:499` (enter + leg).
- **Check-then-send under the monster wire lock, order-only** (6): `aoi.go:464` (the checked
  enters, via `sendMonsterEnter`), `aoi.go:494` (an enter with no leg), `aoi.go:577`
  (`sendMonsterPush`: combat's damage, death and blow, GM `/kill`), `monsterai.go:1735`
  (`sendIfShown`, the AI tick), `monsterai.go:1747` (`sendUnderWireLock`), `monsterlist.go:141`
  (the "not in the world" reply).
- **Fan-out and pushes to other sessions, from handlers, timers and sweeps -- order-only; these
  are the senders that used to wait on a peer** (51): `buffs.go:370,586,595,606`;
  `combat.go:167,197`; `duel.go:310,335,341,466,501,518,523`; `friend.go:414,436`;
  `friendlycast.go:373`; `grounditem.go:284,501,523,529`; `monsterstrike.go:537`; `motion.go:386`;
  `party.go:238`; `regen.go:122`; `trade.go:484,485,493,515,520,525,544,570,588,594,637,669,670,
  677,678,704,705,876,882`; `uniquenotice.go:238`; `useitem.go:870`; `walls.go:487`;
  `world.go:1012,1136,1243,1256,1344`.
- **To the session the code is serving (its handler's replies, its own character's pushes) --
  order-only** (295): `berserkpotion.go:112`; `character.go` (10); `chat.go` (2); `combat.go` (16);
  `composite.go` (6); `deadstate.go` (3); `duel.go` (20); `equipment.go` (13); `friend.go` (25);
  `gm.go` (5); `grounditem.go` (4); `guild.go` (25); `inventory.go` (6); `inventorymove.go` (2);
  `login.go` (2); `monsterstrike.go:531`; `party.go` (17); `quest.go` (8); `register.go` (2);
  `repair.go` (2); `shop.go` (13); `skill.go` (49); `stats.go` (7); `storage.go` (16);
  `teleport.go` (2); `trade.go` (20); `useitem.go` (4); `walls.go:87`; `world.go` (13). The full
  line list is what an AST walk of `server/` prints (the walker is kept out of the repo).
- **Needs a flush before a close: none explicitly.** OpenSRO has no kick, no logout reply
  (`OpLogoutRequest`/`OpLogoutResponse` are defined at `proto/opcodes.go:203-204` and handled
  nowhere) and no shutdown notice (the SIGTERM context sends nothing). The one send-then-close is
  implicit: a handler that sends and then returns an error, which makes the gateway close the
  session -- e.g. `performAttack` after its damage frames when a store write fails
  (`combat.go:1468-1720`), `trade.go:620,663`, `duel.go:419-445`. It is handled once for all in
  `serveConn` by `closeAfterDrain`.

### 3. The limit, from a measurement (MEASURED, render box, `/var/tmp/sendq662/live.sh`)

Round 656's freeze harness on this lane: the branch's server with `-in-memory -single-frame` and
all six monster switches, `-qa-spread-monsters 6000 -qa-spread-radius 5` (about 50 monsters a
region, denser than npcpos's worst region of 35); one real client (int/mob's, the QA sign-in)
entering at the Jangan spawn, `/goto donwhang`, `/goto jangan`, then `/spawnunique` Tiger Girl,
Cerberus and Uruchi, 3.5 min a run. The server logs each session's queue and burst peaks and its
totals at disconnect.

| run | build | busiest 4 s (`send_burst_peak`) | queue peak | writer debt peak | longest write | bytes | closed by the server |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| r1 | limit 4 MB, one write per take | 132,475 | 100,841 | 63.9 µs | 49.7 µs | 1,318,701 | no |
| r2 | limit 1 MB, one write per take | 265,072 | 107,478 | 529 µs | 45.1 µs | 1,144,117 | no |
| r9 | final (2 MB, a frame per write), list forced after the view move (debug delay) | 264,680 | 108,069 | 2.57 ms | 1.09 ms | 1,469,794 | no |
| r10 | final (2 MB, a frame per write) | 133,671 | 99,843 | 719 µs | 662 µs | 1,327,148 | no |

The busiest 4 s is the return to Jangan when the area of interest's view move sends ~1,250
monsters' enters (with their legs) and the list follows (r2: `send burst peak bytes=251756` at
the `/goto jangan`, 265,072 by the end); the queue's peak is the entry's list, queued as one batch.

**`SendQueueLimit` = 2 MB (OURS)**: about 8x the busiest 4 s measured (265,072 bytes -- what a
client frozen 4 s would have queued had the kernel held nothing) and 20x the queue's peak. Over
loopback the kernel buffers take almost everything at once, so the queue's own peak is the one
batch; a real link was not measured (OPEN). r2 ran at 1 MB and was not closed.

### 4. What the live check found: one write per take froze the real client (MEASURED; mitigated here, fixed by the client in round 663)

In r2 and in a repeat (r3), after `/goto jangan` the client drew the ~1,250 pushed monsters and
then processed nothing more -- no list report, no GM reply for `/heal` or the three
`/spawnunique`, which the server logged as executed. The server's writer was never blocked (debt
peak 529 µs). A byte tee of r3's session (a debug build, not committed) parses to its end: 16,660
frames, every one intact and in order, the list's three pages and motion page contiguous
(frames 8178-8181), the GM replies at 15008-15009. So the client stopped reading. `ss -tmi` on
the box during the same freeze (r8):

```
client  ESTAB 31250 0  127.0.0.1:55800 127.0.0.1:16662  skmem:(r137152,rb138172,...,d11) rcvmss:52224
server  ESTAB 0 144311 127.0.0.1:16662 127.0.0.1:55800  backoff:6 bytes_retrans:11761
```

The client's receive buffer is full (137,152 of 138,172 bytes of kernel memory) holding only
31,250 bytes of data, and the server is backing off against a shut window. `packet_reader.gd`
reads a frame's payload only once `get_available_bytes()` covers all of it; the frame due was a
32,735-byte list page. The branch wrote everything it took in one write, which loopback carries
as a few ~52 KB segments (`rcvmss:52224`); a segment read part-way is charged its whole memory
until it is read to its end, so the buffer filled before a whole page was in it, and each side
waited on the other. It needs the view move to beat the list request (the 100 ms reconcile tick
against the client's ~15 ms): with a debug-only 60 ms delay in the list handler forcing that
order, the base (int/mob 1ea6b02, r7) came through (`server reports 1259 monster(s)`, every GM
reply) and the one-write branch (r8) froze.

The writer now writes a frame per write (`writeFrames`), as the synchronous Send did. That
**mitigates** the wedge; it does not fix it (round 662's review): a frame per write keeps a frame
in segments of its own only while the socket's send queue is drained. Once it is backlogged --
the client's window shut, as it is while a load freezes the client's main thread -- Linux's
`tcp_sendmsg` appends each new write into the unsent tail skb, up to its size goal (~64 KB over
loopback), so frames coalesce into large segments however they were written, and the same wedge
can recur. The fix is the client's reader, done in round 663. `TestTheWriterWritesAFramePerWrite`
pins the mitigation (with one write per take: `5 frames went out in 1
writes, want one write per frame`). With the fix and the same forced order
(r9) the client came through: `server reports 1251 monster(s)` after the return, every GM reply,
the three uniques spawned and listed. The final build without the delay (r10): world entry `server
reports 1286 monster(s)`, back in Jangan `1249`, the three uniques, every GM reply; server RSS 80
MB, 1.1 % CPU; the only disconnect is the script killing the client (`connection reset by peer`);
no `session send stalled` line in any run.

The client's reader has the latent fault whatever the server does: a frame is only read once its
whole payload fits in the socket's buffer, so anything that fills that buffer with partly-read
segments can wedge it. Its fix -- read what is available into its own buffer -- was made in
round 663.

### 5. Tests

**NEGATIVE against int/mob 1ea6b02** (a second worktree; the new test files copied in, with
`sendqueue662_setup_test.go` replaced by a stub whose `sendBatch` sends frame by frame; MEASURED):

```

    sendqueue662_test.go:191: the slow reader was never closed: the fan-out wrote to it for 5 s
--- FAIL: TestASlowReaderNeverHoldsTheSender (6.03s)

    sendqueue662_test.go:261: a fan-out pass took 52ms: it waited on the slow reader
--- FAIL: TestASlowReaderIsClosedByItsWritersBudget (0.77s)

    sendqueue662_test.go:362: 26 single frames landed inside a batch
--- FAIL: TestSendBatchIsNeverInterleaved (0.87s)
--- PASS: TestTheFramesBeforeAHandlersErrorAreDelivered (0.01s)
--- PASS: TestNoGoroutineLeakAcrossConnectDisconnect (0.24s)
FAIL	github.com/OpenSRO/OpenSRO/server/internal/gateway	7.923s

    sendqueue662_test.go:57: only 260 of 1000 ticks ran in 5 s
    sendqueue662_test.go:60: the longest tick took 9.954s: the tick waited on the client that does not read
--- FAIL: TestASlowClientNeverHoldsTheAITick (10.34s)
FAIL	github.com/OpenSRO/OpenSRO/server/internal/session	10.340s
```

The two that pass on the base pass because the base writes synchronously (it has nothing to
drain and no writer to leak); they pin what the queue must keep. The drain test was checked
against the branch with the drain cut (`SendDrainTimeout` = 0): `frame 0 of 41: EOF -- the
session was closed before its queue was written`.

- `TestASlowReaderNeverHoldsTheSender` (gateway): 100 frames of 16 KB to a client reading 1.6 MB/s
  through a 16 KB send buffer return in 1.9-7.4 ms; a fan-out to it and a fast client never
  waits (longest pass 0.2-0.3 ms); the slow client is closed by its queue limit; the fast one gets
  every frame.
- `TestASlowReaderIsClosedByItsWritersBudget`: the limit out of reach, budget 300 ms: closed at a
  writer debt of 300 ms after ~380 ms, longest fan-out pass 0.17-0.25 ms.
- `TestASlowClientNeverHoldsTheAITick` (session): the real `monsterAI.deliver` to two TCP clients
  watching one cell, one never reading: 1,000 ticks of a 16 KB push, the longest 1.5 ms; the
  reading client gets all 1,000; the other is closed.
- `TestAPeerThatFreezesThenReadsIsNotClosed` (round 656's, kept with the production budget and
  limit): the fan-out is now paced (16 KB every 100 ms, 640 KB over the freeze), since a flat-out
  loop no longer paces itself by blocking; the server's send buffer is cut to 16 KB so the writer
  really is blocked through the freeze. Debt peak 2.9-3.5 s, not closed, every frame received in
  order, no send over 0.4 ms.
- `TestSendBatchIsNeverInterleaved`: 20 batches of 20 against 400 singles through a full socket:
  no single inside a batch, both streams in order.
- `TestTheFramesBeforeAHandlersErrorAreDelivered`: a handler queues 40 frames of 16 KB and a last
  frame, then returns an error: the client reads all 41 in order, then EOF.
- `TestTheWriterWritesAFramePerWrite`: five frames queued together (a batch of three with a
  full-size page, two single sends) go out in five writes, each byte for byte its frame (§4).
- `TestNoGoroutineLeakAcrossConnectDisconnect`: 1,000 connect/disconnect cycles, one in ten
  hanging up with 256 KB queued and unread: 4 goroutines before, 4 after, every session's writer
  returned and its queue nil.
- Round 656's `TestSendGivesUpOnAStalledClient` now paces its sender and puts the limit out of
  reach: every Send returns at once, the writer's deadline closes the session, then
  `ErrSendStalled` at once and the disconnect. `TestASlowSteadyReaderIsClosedWithinItsBudget`
  paces its fan-out (a flat-out loop outran even the fast reader and passed its queue limit); it passes as
  before.
- `cd server && go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 -p 1 ./...`: 61 packages ok,
  exit 0 (the final code; an earlier run fell in the dev machine's disk-full window, when Postgres
  was down, and was re-run). `go test -race -count=1` on gateway and on session's AOI, stress,
  sleep, GM-kill, damage-guard, monster-list, unique-notice and panicking-push tests plus the tick
  test (33 tests): ok, no data race.

### 6. Open (docs/TODO.md)

- The client's `packet_reader.gd` waits for a whole payload in the kernel buffer (§4): a client-lane
  fix.
- The limit (2 MB) and the drain (2 s) are OURS. The limit was sized from loopback; a real link,
  and a crowded town with many players moving, were not measured.
- A future kick, logout reply or shutdown notice must end the session through the gateway's
  drain, not `Session.Close`, or its last frame is dropped.
- `Send` now returns nil for a frame that a later close never delivers. No caller acted on a nil
  error as "delivered"; a future one must not.

### 7. Review follow-up (round 662's adversarial review; merged with int/mob d60c8c3: rounds 659 and 660)

- **The merge with round 659 (M1).** 659 put a monster's status between its enter and its leg in
  `sendMonsterEnter`, which 662 had made one batch. The conflict's obvious resolution -- keep both
  sides -- compiles and sends every enter twice. Resolved instead with a builder:
  `monsterStatusPacket(id)` returns the monster's OpObjectStatus (or nil) where 659's
  `sendMonsterStatus` sent it, and `sendMonsterEnter` queues ONE `SendBatch` of (enter, status if
  any, leg if walking). The list does the same: 659's deferred `sendStatusesOfList` becomes
  `statusPacketsOfList`, appended to the list's own batch after the pages and motion pages, still
  under the wire lock. Every other status send of 659 (`pushMonsterStatus`, `broadcastStatus`) is a
  single frame, and 660's `monsterSnapshotFor` only shapes a record inside those two sequences, so
  no other site needed the rule. `TestAnEnteringMonsterWithAStatusIsOneEnterThenStatusThenLeg`:
  2,000 enters of a bleeding, walking monster race 20,000 filler frames to one session
  (`GOMAXPROCS(4)` so the OS interleaves the senders even on a one-core host); every enter is
  followed by its status, then its leg, and exactly 2,000 enters arrive. Negatives (MEASURED):

  ```
  keep-both resolution:
    sendqueue662r_test.go:83: enter 1 was followed by 0x3057 then 0x007e; want OpObjectStatus (0x3057) then OpMonsterMoved (0x007c)
    sendqueue662r_test.go:102: 150 enters arrived for 200 sent, 300 sequences broken
  659's separate Sends (enter, status, leg):
    sendqueue662r_test.go:88: enter 103 was followed by 0x3057 then 0x7ffd; want OpObjectStatus (0x3057) then OpMonsterMoved (0x007c)
    sendqueue662r_test.go:107: 2000 enters arrived for 2000 sent, 5 sequences broken
  ```
  (The first was run at the test's earlier size of 200 enters.)
- **A frame per write mitigates the client wedge; it does not fix it (M2).** §4 and `writeFrames`'
  comment now say so and why: under a backlog `tcp_sendmsg` coalesces writes into the unsent tail
  skb. The fix is the client's reader, done in round 663.
- **The rolling byte and checksum follow wire order (L1).** Nothing tested a session with
  `SetSecurity` (it has no production caller yet), so drawing the byte outside the queue lock
  passed every test. `TestRollingByteAndChecksumFollowWireOrder`: 8 goroutines x 500 Sends with
  real generators, read back with generators seeded the same. Against that mutant (encode outside
  `outMu`, append under it): `after 41 of 4000 frames: proto: rolling byte mismatch for opcode
  0x006b: got 0x3e, want 0x6c`. The code was already right; the test keeps it so.
- **The queue limit is checked before the frames are queued (L2).** Until now the batch was
  encoded and appended, then the total compared, so a queue could hold more than the limit, and a
  single batch bigger than the limit closed a session whose queue was empty. Now a batch that would
  take a NON-EMPTY queue past `SendQueueLimit` closes the session without encoding anything (no
  rolling byte drawn); a batch into an empty queue is always taken (nothing is piling up behind
  it; the next Send while it waits is then over). `TestTheQueueLimitBoundsAGrowingQueueNotOneBatch`
  against the round's first commit:

  ```
  sendqueue662r_test.go:72: a 98319-byte batch into an empty queue (limit 65536): gateway: session stalled: ...
  (its first half cut) sendqueue662r_test.go:80: the queue held 65560 bytes, past its 65536-byte limit, before the session was closed
  ```
- **A partner's Send error no longer closes the sender's session (L3; older than round 662).**
  An AST walk of every non-test `.Send`/`.SendBatch` in `server/` (the only callers are in
  `internal/session` and `internal/gateway`) found 13 handlers returning ANOTHER session's Send
  error as their own, which closes the session they serve: `duel.go` (challenge invite, decline,
  start, damage, end), `friend.go` (request, accept), `trade.go` (invite, decline, start, offer
  update, completed, cancelled). With the queue those errors are `ErrSendStalled` for a partner
  given up for its sends and `ErrSessionClosed` for one leaving; before it, a write timeout or a
  closed socket, after a wait of up to 10 s. Each now goes through `sendToPeer` (`peersend.go`),
  which drops the error: the gateway has already logged the partner's stall and closes the
  partner's own connection. The walk finds none left.
  `TestAStalledTradePartnerDoesNotDisconnectTheSender`: Bram stops reading and his queue passes
  its limit; Aria changes her offer twice and gets both results. With the offer update's
  `return other.Session.Send(...)` put back: `tradepeer662_test.go:56: Write: write tcp ...: write:
  broken pipe` (Aria's connection was closed after the first).
- **Runs.** `go build ./... && go vet ./... && go test -count=1 -p 1 -timeout 30m ./...`: 62
  packages ok, exit 0. `go test -race`: gateway ok (11 s); session with
  `-run 'AOI|Unique|MonsterList|Send|Stress|Status|Nest'` ok (245 s), no data race. Server-only,
  so no performance gate.

## Six-hundred-and-sixty-first round: each unique stands at one of its spots, comes back at another after its real wait, fights with its own skills -- and Cerberus summons its Ladons

The user (2026-09-30): "Make sure this includes uniques as well where they spawn on their usual
rotation at one of their possible spots. Make sure the uniques spawn additional mobs if that's what
they did." The reading is `docs/protocol/monster_ai.md`, "The unique rotation and the minions
(round 661)"; the operator's side is `deploy/README.md`, "The full map (round 660)".

Labels: READ (SR_GameServer.exe: the dump, `srv.asm`, `objdump -s`), MEASURED, INFERRED, OURS, and
EXTERNAL for the user's shard DB (the Eternity backup, round 658). No DB row, CSV or game data is in
this commit; the tests use synthetic rows.

### 1. What shipped (MEASURED at boot on the render box: npcpos + characterdata of our archive, the shard's CSVs)

Under `-full-map` with `-nest-db-dir`, each field unique's npcpos spots are the nests of its shard
hive (total 1, EXTERNAL), and the READ rotation runs them:

Every spot joins its own species' nest (the join's 1.0-unit tolerance; round 660 measured every
nest within 0.00014); the `_STR` twins' hives on the same spots are never placed. One boot's join:

the Pharaoh temple left out** (their nests' hives are worlds 57-59, below); **1 rank-8 row left out**
(MOB_SD_APIS); 10,104 nests placed (4,063 matched, 2,346 swapped with their own tactics, 3,695
swapped stand-ins); 17 capped hives (round 660's 10 plus the seven unique hives); at most 34,384
alive. The boot log writes one `unique rotation` line per unique, and each `unique hatched`,
`unique rotation: re-pinned` and `unique summons`.

`-unique-respawn=<dur>` (env `OPENSRO_UNIQUE_RESPAWN`, OURS, testing) replaces the uniques' wait;
`-nest-respawn` no longer reaches them. The two new DB files (`Tab_RefAISkill.csv`, `_RefSkill.csv`)
are optional: without them the uniques rotate and fight but summon nothing, and the boot log says so.

### 2. What was READ this round

- **The rotation.** Build pin `CMainProcess::FUN_0055efe0`: a hive of one nest pins it; a hive of
  two or more throws `abs(rand()) % n` and pins NOTHING -- its loop re-enters past the compare
  (0x55f041..0x55f05f; *corrected by the review, section 8: this line read `nests[abs(rand()) % n]`*)
  -- so the first appearance after a boot is the hive's first due nest, nests[0]. Re-pin `AI::CNest::FUN_0055eec0` (asm 0x55eec0..0x55efce): only when the capped hive was
  full before the death; `k = abs(rand()) % (n+1)`, clamped to n-1 -- the last nest comes up twice as
  often as any other, kept -- and EVERY nest of the hive re-armed (`RearmHatchTimer` 0x560e50:
  stamp now, a fresh uniform [col12, col13] roll; the pinned nest throws one roll more, discarded,
  at 0x55ef7a). The re-arm is any capped hive's, not only a total-1 one: round 660's ten capped
  hives now wait a window from a loss out of a full hive too (a correction to round 660).
- **Rank 8** (the coordinator's check): fourteen of the fifteen rarity-8 field rows, with OSIRIS_3
  (rarity 3), are the Pharaoh temple's bosses (SPHINX, SEKHMET, NEPHTHYS, HORUS, OSIRIS, three
  variants each). Their nests sit in hives of GameWorldID 57/58/59, which the DB's

  (y 114-124, x 179-196), each a single nest of cap 1 on a 10,800 s window in an uncapped hive -- no
